note: Optimize demo/the_dogfooding.py's collisions_at_bar from N × memory.lookup(limit=50) to a direct pairwise scan with SequenceMatcher length-ratio and quick_ratio bailouts against the seal bar. 82s → 23s (~3.6×) on the whole demo, ~36× on the collisions function alone.

decisions.question: How should collisions_at_bar be sped up so the demo does not keep pushing against the CI timeout as the corpus grows?
decisions.commitment: Route by matcher shape. For a StringMatcher-shaped matcher (no `score()` method), a new `_collisions_via_ratio_bailout` fetches candidate rows once, and for each decision uses SequenceMatcher's length-ratio and quick_ratio as O(1) and O(N) upper bounds respectively; a candidate whose upper bound is below memory.SEAL_THRESHOLD (0.92) is skipped before the expensive `ratio()` call. Local measurement on the 532-row dogfood corpus: 46.6s → ~1.3s for the collisions function; 82s → 23s for the whole demo. For a `score()`-based matcher (DefectMatcher, semantic backends), the upper bounds do not apply — the dispatcher falls back to `_collisions_via_lookup` which preserves the original N × memory.lookup path. The public entry point `collisions_at_bar` picks between them via `uses_raw_score(matcher)`. Output shape preserved: sorted by decision, then by similarity descending within a decision, capped at 50 per decision to match `memory.lookup(limit=50)`'s truncation; similarity rounded to 3 decimals as `memory.lookup` does. Two tests hold this down (tests/test_dogfooding_collisions.py): byte-for-byte equivalence on a controlled fixture, and a synthetic-corpus test asserting fast finds ≥ what slow finds AND runs faster.
decisions.why: The 82s → 180s CI wall was going to be hit again — the demo does an O(N²) sweep over a corpus that grows every PR. The previous fix (bumping the CI subprocess timeout from 180s → 300s in c33786e) was a band-aid the survey of the last 20 merged PRs showed we would keep having to widen: 17 of 20 PRs touch a demo-relevant path (14 add decision files, 3 touch matcher/memory/cascade code), so the demo actually re-measures something on almost every PR and skipping-in-CI would give up real signal. The real fix is at the compute, not the timeout — an O(1) length bail plus an O(N) quick_ratio bail knocks out ~98% of pairs before the O(N²) SequenceMatcher.ratio() runs. That is what the upper-bound predicates in difflib are for, and they were being ignored by the general-purpose memory.lookup path (which cannot use them: it has to return top-K by absolute similarity, not top-K-above-a-threshold).
decisions.doors_closed: Bumping the timeout further as the corpus grows (a ratchet the survey showed we would keep tightening). Sample-and-full CI (skips the measurement on some PRs, but the survey showed most PRs change what the demo measures). Optimizing memory.lookup itself with the same bailouts (the general lookup cannot use them — it has to return the top-K by absolute similarity, not the top-K-above-a-threshold, so a bail-at-bar predicate would miss below-bar-but-top-K candidates the caller might want).

decisions.question: Should the fast path exactly match memory.lookup's top-50-then-filter semantics, or its own filter-then-top-50?
decisions.commitment: Filter-then-top-50. `memory.lookup(limit=50)` returns the top 50 candidates by similarity irrespective of the seal bar; the demo then filters those 50 by `>= SEAL_THRESHOLD`. On a corpus where a query has 50+ hits above the bar, `memory.lookup`'s truncation drops some real collisions. The fast path's filter-then-top-50 preserves all above-bar hits (up to 50) — a strictly more honest count. On the shipped 532-row dogfood corpus this is a distinction without a difference (no decision has 50 above-bar collisions), so byte-for-byte equivalence holds. On a pathological 200-row synthetic test corpus with dense above-bar hits the fast path finds strictly more; the corresponding test asserts fast ⊇ slow rather than fast == slow and comments on the semantic difference.
decisions.why: Matching top-50-then-filter would defeat the whole point of the bailouts — they only work when the threshold is fixed (the seal bar). Preserving the general shape of `memory.lookup` here would require running the O(N²) ratio on every candidate below the bar, cancelling the speedup. Filter-first is the correct semantics for a threshold-based query anyway (top-K-above-bar, not top-K-then-bar-filter); the two agree wherever the truncation is not binding, and the shipped corpus is exactly that case.
